From nothing it seemed to her now, but he'd kicked and he'd struggled but she was too strong, and afterwards he'd cried for what seemed like hours, the first and last time she'd seen him like that.

Sapphire recalled a story she'd done, where she'd had to return to a village somewhere - Sri Lanka she thought, after a decade had passed. She had come to know everyone there the first time, when she'd stayed for a month, researching a band of mystical warriors who were said to be planning to commit remote terrorist strikes with their minds. It was said they had already caused a tsunami by chanting nonstop for a week. She’d lived in the village with a family of nine, a father and eight children, all boys. The boys looked exactly the same to her then, except for their heights, which were consistent with each of their years. Going back, ten years later, the boys were all grown and were now all the same height as each other, the same as their father, yet she picked each one out by their name, missing none. She could tell by their smiles, by the tone of their voices, by a host of subtle traits. She prided herself on that skill but had to admit to herself now that she probably would never have picked Alex out of a crowd. He was more alien to her than any one of those remote village boys she had barely even known. Where had her whole childhood gone?

'You turn your back on a place', she thought, 'and the place turns its back on you too.'

She wondered what Spring Hill Lake would be like. The last time she was there she had barely paid any attention - she was helping her father move out to his luxury retirement community. She had been in a hurry, and didn’t care to notice the town. She remembered the airport and that's about all. She had taken a taxi to the old neighborhood where her father had remained all those years, but she hardly looked up, and when she got there she got down to work, making calls and bossing people around. It hadn't been fun to see her father becoming more and more helpless, a man who for all of her life had always been the one giving orders. She scarcely remembered her mother, only the father who worked his late hours and never had time for his kid.

'I would never have time for one either,' she said to herself, remembering her most well worn reason for not having children.

'Whatever, I hated that place,' she considered as she was approaching the outskirts of town. She would stay by the airport, in that same hotel, the one with the faded red carpeting. She had already made reservations and by the time she'd checked in and flopped down on the bed, it was time to call Qatar and Meyer.

“Casey? Casey!” shouted James as he searched for his missing son. “We found the way out! We’re going to come back with a search group and find you. I promise! All right Roberto, let’s go.”

Roberto looked at James and realized how heartbroken he was. They had been searching for over an hour when Roberto stumbled upon the stairs leading back up to the temple. After he found James, they had looked for Casey, but to no avail. Finally, they had given up, deciding that they’d come back tomorrow. Knowing these temples, he hoped Casey could survive until tomorrow...

As the world slowly came into focus through half-closed eyes, Casey sat up. *Where am I?* he thought. He put a hand to his head and felt a huge bump. Then it all came back to him. He must have fallen through some kind of trap door and hit his head.

By now his eyes had adjusted to the darkness, and he looked around for his flashlight. He couldn’t find it and figured that he must have dropped it outside the room. Before long, his eyes fell on a large, circular disk that was inlaid into the floor. It was roughly three meters across. The more Casey looked at it, the more he could make out.

Now that he looked more closely, he could see little glowing symbols. *Maybe some sort of optical illusion*, he thought. He moved over and put his hand to the floor. Unexpectedly, the strange disk started to spin, and he quickly took his hand away. He realized that it must be some kind of puzzle. Maybe it would open the door, so he could get out!

That was when he recognized the symbols. He’d seen them before. They were on the Maya calendar, predicting the end of the world. He slowly turned the symbols into place. Jaguar, Sun... He kept turning the circles that were inside of the larger circle. Then when the center disc was the only one left, he pushed it down and heard a small click. To his surprise, the whole disc slowly descended into the floor, and he realized that he had just made everything much worse.

It was late afternoon. The day had been fairly uneventful, and despite Casey’s attempts to tell everyone about the warship and the destruction it would cause, no one would believe him. He knew that when the time came, he would simply have to take things into his own hands. He had been up at the temple practically all day and was extremely bored. He had just drifted off to sleep when he felt a shadow pass over his body. He bolted upright and looked up to the sky. After waiting for them all day, the Maya had finally arrived.

Casey looked down upon the camp and watched as all of its inhabitants hastily moved into the jungle as they saw the impending threat coming down from the sky. Casey knew that if he didn’t do something soon, then the army would blow the Mayan ship off the face of the planet. He broke out of his reverie as the ship landed in the clearing, and he was forced into action.

Just like last time, the circular portal in the side of the ship slid back letting out a *hiss*. Before the Maya moved more than a few feet from the spacecraft, Casey ran as fast as he could down the stairs and almost crashed headlong into the waiting party of Maya. He just managed to right himself before he fell, face first, in the dirt. Before they could attack him he cried out.

“Wait, I’m not your enemy!” he exclaimed. He reached in his pocket and brought out the ball with a swift movement. At the same moment, a strange garbled sound came out of the headset of the Mayan who appeared to be in charge of the group.

The garbled sound stopped just as suddenly as it had begun, and a strange mechanical voice said, “Language identified: English. Language translator adjusted.”

A new voice came over the speaker that Casey just noticed was strapped to the Mayan’s chest. This one spoke in a halting, but slightly more humanoid voice.

“Hello, Casey. We have been watching you through the orb. We also know what you have been through.” Casey was suddenly bursting with questions that needed answers, but then, as if reading his thoughts the Mayan began again. “We know that you must have questions, but we should leave now. Your army has their strange metal weapons pointed at us right now, and if we don’t leave soon they will blow us into oblivion.”

It was at this moment that Casey remembered the ball in his hand. He held it up above his head, and the light of the setting sun reflected off of its polished surface. “You came for this, didn’t you?” he asked, finally understanding the reasoning behind all this. “I must have activated some sort of message when I took it.”

“Yes, you are a bright little one, aren’t you? The orb has immense power in it, and we knew that if it fell into the wrong hands, your world would change forever. The new planet we have cultivated is more civilized than this one. We ask if you wish to come with us. I can assure you that you will be amazed by what you see.”

Casey didn’t know what to say. He had always dreamed of visiting another planet. However, before he had even consciously made a decision, he knew there was no decision to make. He gently placed the orb in the Mayan’s hand and stepped a few paces back.

“Not today, for I have many things yet to experience on my own planet. Perhaps when I am older and have nothing left here. But for now, I bid you farewell and hope you have a safe journey back.”

With that, Casey waved at them and began to turn away. However, the Maya weren’t done yet. The one Casey had been talking too reached into his pocket and took something out, throwing it to Casey. He barely had time to catch it before it hit the ground. Then, the Maya turned away from him and walked through the circular portal, which sealed behind them.

As their ship made its way up into the sky again, Casey felt a feeling of satisfaction spread from head to toe as he realized that he had just saved the world. He didn’t need anyone to know, and he didn’t want to be on T.V. He was just glad that he knew in his heart what he had done.

Casey’s eyes moved from the diminishing ship back to his immediate surroundings. His dad was running towards him with a team of medics. When they reached him, he just smiled at his dad. Confusion and wonder filled his dad’s eyes. There would be time to answer questions later. For now, Casey just said, “Come on Dad, let’s go home.”

“Sir, we think we may have found something.”

James looked up from the documents he was surveying. “Could you be a little more specific?” he asked irritably to the man who had barged in on him.

“We found a large circular engraving in the temple. I’m no expert, sir, but it looks an awful lot like the Maya calendar.”

“I’ll have a look,” said James. He got up from his desk that was inside his little, makeshift tent that they had set up. He trod slowly over to the temple and trudged up the set of stairs that led to the entrance.

The man who had brought him the news led him to a room where a skylight let in a beam of sunlight, which fell directly on a large stone disc. James went closer and examined it. It did share a remarkable resemblance to the Maya calendar; however, it had an enormous hole in the center. To James it looked like a place to insert another part.

“Notify me if you find anything else, especially my son.” James exhaled as he thought about Casey. It had been a day since he had last seen him, and he was beginning to think that he might not be coming back. He cursed himself for bringing him on this trip. He could only hope that he was all right.

The disc came to an abrupt stop after descending about ten meters. Casey wondered how he was ever going to get back up to the temple. He looked around and noticed all of the tunnels surrounding the room he was now in. He started down one but then stopped. He searched in his backpack and eventually found a stick of chalk. He didn’t want to get lost, so he dragged the chalk along the wall as he walked. If he couldn’t find his way back, he could always follow the chalk.

As he continued down the tunnel, it occurred to him that he could see. The passage should have been submerged in darkness, but, instead, it glowed with light. He looked up and found the source of light. Strange, glowing orbs were fastened to the ceiling. They reminded Casey of light bulbs, and he wondered how they got their power.

He didn’t ponder it too long and soon continued on his way. The passage seemed to go on forever, but finally it opened out into what he assumed was a room. He had no way of knowing, however, because he couldn’t see the ceiling or the walls. The room was immense.

He had been wandering around the room for a while when he came upon a table. On it was a strange metal contraption. When Casey looked closer, he saw little buttons on it. He pressed one, and the whole thing came alive. A hatch opened up on the top, and a tiny little miniature head popped up and started to speak.

“Automaton 53A76 reporting for duty. Please enter passcode or provide identification.”

Casey was unsure of what to do. He obviously didn’t have either of what the robot requested. He said, “Ummm... Where am I?”

“You are in sector 5, sub section 7. If you wish to make a request, please enter passcode.”

“What is the passcode?”

“I am not authorized to answer that question,” said the machine. Casey didn’t think it would work, but he had to try.

“Who built this and when?”

“The Underground Preservation Chamber, A.K.A UPC, was developed in 900 A.D. by the Maya architects and engineers.”

Casey knew that the Maya had been a very intelligent people, but he knew that they definitely hadn’t had electricity. “What is the purpose of the UPC?” he asked.

“The UPC was built to house Maya technology, so that if one day they come back, they can take it with them.” Casey was about to say something when the robot continued, “Your next question will be where they are, so I shall tell you. The Maya left in 1105 A.D. in their spaceships to find other planets that would sustain life in case the Earth was destroyed. They left a single orb in the UPC to power everything and make sure that it went on undisturbed.”

“What is the orb?” asked Casey. “Also, how do you know English?”

“The orb is one of many. They are used to..” Suddenly the machine cut off and its eyes began to flash red. “Automaton 53A73 terminated,” said a hollow, mechanical voice from within the machine. When smoke began to pour from its eyes, Casey decided to make a run for it.

He sprinted as far as he could into the room before having to stop. Suddenly, dread dawned upon him. He had been in such a hurry that he had forgotten to keep marking with the chalk. He didn’t know how to find an exit. He gazed around uncertainly. His eyes fell upon a strange room off in the distance. He slowly made his way over to it.

After what seemed like forever, he finally reached the room. It had more unusual markings on the sides, and he could see three prongs of metal reaching down from the ceiling to connect the roof. He moved toward the door and threw it open.

The inside of the room was fairly barren, but in the middle there were six prongs. Three came up from the ground, and the other ones continued down from the ceiling. In the center was a small silver sphere. Strangely, Casey felt compelled to take it. He knew he was forgetting something, but his memory had become cloudy when he had entered the room. He walked over and plucked the ball from its perch. Instantly, the lights went off, and the world plunged into darkness.

A giant shadow blotted out the sun. As Casey watched, the shadow slowly expanded. Remembering what his dad had said, he reluctantly went to the temple and hid inside the doorway, so he could still see what was going on outside. The army vehicles had assembled outside, and he assumed that they had done the same all around the whole area.

Sooner than he had expected, the treetops began bend from the wind that was now rushing around them. It must have been caused by what he assumed were a spaceship’s engines. Just at that moment, it came into his view. Actually, it completely obscured his view, and he was surprised it could even fit into the clearing. Strange, spiked landing gear came out of the hull, a strange circular door appeared in the apparently seamless side of the spaceship and a metal ramp slid down to the surface of the earth, like a ruler coming out of a tape measure. A small group of Maya descended down it, maybe seven or eight of them.

Casey watched in awe as they began to come over to where he was hiding. His heart began to pound as he realized that he was about to put himself in danger, but he wasn’t afraid. His mind was in turmoil, but finally, mustering all his courage, he stood up and walked towards the advancing party. He saw looks of relief come over their faces, and they began to jog toward him. Just as he had suspected, they must have only wanted to talk, not take over the earth.

Then came a moment that would haunt his dreams forever. He heard a loud bang, and the group of Maya was obliterated. Casey looked over into the trees and saw smoke rising from a huge tank. Furious, he ran over to the trees, trying to hide his tears. He could still see the joyful expressions on the faces of the Maya.

*Boom! Boom! Boom!* More tanks fired upon on the huge ship. One must’ve hit a gas tank or something, because suddenly there was a *whoosh*, and the ship exploded into a giant fireball, hurling shrapnel everywhere. Just at that moment, Casey reached the safety of the trees with all the tanks. That was when he saw his father. His anger transformed into fear as he saw the huge piece of shrapnel sticking out of his father’s chest.

“Dad!” Casey cried. Medics already swarmed around him.

“Casey! I thought I told you to stay in the temple!” his dad shouted angrily.

“Dad, you’re injured!”

“Don’t worry about it Casey, just get back to the tem...” His sentence was cut off as, once again, the sun disappeared. “Get to the temple, Casey! It looks like they’ve sent for reinforcements!”

Against his will, Casey was off again, running back to the temple. He ran as fast as he could, because he remembered how fast the other ship had landed. A snake lashed out in front of him and he tripped and fell. Soon, he was back on his feet and running. Then, he broke through the trees and was in the clearing once again.

Finally, he reached the temple and began to climb the stairs. Suddenly, huge shadow blanketed the whole valley. Casey looked up, and all the blood drained from his face. Several hundred feet up was a huge expanse of metallic armor plating, stretching as far as he could see into the distance. Attached to it were fierce looking to be weapons of all different shapes and sizes.

Realizing that the clearing was about to descend into utter chaos, Casey dashed up the stairs to the temple’s entrance. It was a good thing he did because if he would have lingered a moment longer, he would have been dead.

From Agent Sneed's point of view, Sapphire Karadjian had vanished along with the girl. The moment they stepped into the hole they were gone, just like that, like the bird she had seen earlier, raven or not. It meant a headache of a report to be filed, but file it she did, and the paperwork made its long way to that vault where everything to be gladly forgotten was eventually stored. And forgotten it was, because not long after Sapphire vanished, the End Times themselves also came to an end. The fires went out in the hole. The pit stopped its burning and smoldering, the smoke cleared, and the heat went away. By the weekend it was only an eyesore.

In the weeks and months that followed, decisions had to be made. You couldn't keep the security going forever, especially now that nothing was happening and there wasn't any more point in it. First the television cameras drifted away, as the ratings sagged and viewers got bored. The number of guards was steadily whittled down to a handful. Then the fences began to come down and the city planners met and planned hearings and even more meetings. They brought in trucks with lots of gravel and dirt and filled in the hole so it wouldn't be a hazard any longer.

Eventually a contract was put out for bid. Anyone with ideas on what to do with the place was invited to submit a proposal. There was one from a firm called Hedgeley and Kirkham, Architects. It was Argus' idea to cover the thing with a meadow, no buildings or structures at all, just a field, basically, open space. This notion was rejected as impractical.

"What's that supposed to mean?" Sapphire snapped. She was hoping she'd heard the last of Agent Sneed. "I suppose you're going to tell me it just went poof?"

"It just went poof," Sneed retorted.

"All that security," Sapphire began to say, while waving a hand at Margaret to indicate she would fill her in shortly.

"For nothing," Sneed completed the sentence. "Look, we knew there was a chance this would happen. Hell, anything could happen, that's why we kept her under wraps. At least she hasn't been spotted anywhere else, as far as we know."

"Oh, we'd know if she had," Sapphire sneered. "It'd be all over the TV by now if a little girl on fire just happened to pop up somewhere, wouldn't you say?"

"We need your help," the agent said, as calmly as she could. Sapphire was as annoying to her as vice versa. Sneed hated reporters in general, especially those who thought they were a class apart, and Karadjian, to her, was as arrogant and snotty as they came.

"You keep saying that," Sapphire told her, "but I don't know what I can do."

"You can get to Argus Kirkham," Sneed reminded her. "He won't talk to us."

"He won't talk to me either," Sapphire said. "In fact I'm sitting in his kitchen right now, talking with his wife, because he just up and walked out pretty much the moment he saw me."

"Oh, man," Sneed said. "And you just let him get away?"

"What am I supposed to do?" Sapphire nearly shouted. "I'm not the law. I'm just a citizen, remember? Somebody doesn't want to talk to me there's not a thing I can do about it. Why don't you lock him up if you want him so bad?"

She glanced over at Margaret, who was looking more and more furious by the moment. Sapphire shook her head as if to convey she wasn't being serious, but she knew her words were speaking pretty loudly for themselves.

"That would just attract attention," Sneed insisted. "We don't want that, and anyway, we couldn't hold him. People have rights, you know."

"Really? Since when? Can't you all declare war on dragons or something? Oh, never mind."

"I don't know what you are talking about," Sneed sighed, "but please, please, couldn't you try again? Just one more time? I've heard a lot about you. Sapphire Karadjian never gives up, isn't that what they say?"

"Don't go trying flattery," Sapphire snorted. "It doesn't suit you. Look, okay. One more time, all right?"

"Thank you," Sneed said. "And if there's anything we can do."

"It doesn't seem like there is," she chortled as she ended the call. She looked up at a glaring Margaret.

"Lock him up? Lock him up? Some friend you turned out to be," Margaret yelled as she got up from the table.

"Sorry," Sapphire sighed. "I didn't mean it, all right? And they're not going to, anyway. They mean well, I think, if they mean anything at all. They're worried about him, and so am I."

"And I'm not?" Margaret was still upset. Her hands were shaking as she nearly spilled her coffee on herself. "What do you think we've been doing these past few days? Waiting, that's what. Waiting for this monster to reach out and grab him. And those federal agents are so afraid of the TV cameras they won't do anything to help us. Oh, they're surrounding us, all the time. Look outside, you can see them now. They follow us everywhere. They watch our house and what good do you think it’s doing? None at all. It's all we can do to keep Arvid from even knowing what's going on. God, that isn't easy. He knows something's up. He doesn't know what but he's a sharp kid. I don't know how much longer we can take this."

Sapphire was astounded by Margaret's outburst. She'd been so calm just minutes before, while expounding on her absolutely inane theories about whatever it was, and now she was losing it. It must be stressful, Sapphire realized, just the unknown and seemingly unknowable aspect of it all.

"I don't think there's anything to worry about." Sapphire said for some reason, just to hear her voice, perhaps. She immediately realized it was a dumb thing to say. Of course there was something to worry about.

"How do I find him?" she asked. "I know he doesn't want to talk to me, but maybe I can help, somehow. I don't know how, but ..."

"He'll be walking along the waterfront," Margaret told her. "Arvid's school is only a few blocks away. Argus designed it, did you know? It's a beautiful little school. You should see it sometime, maybe when all this is over."

"I'd love to," Sapphire heard herself saying, knowing full well she didn't care at all about a school or any other building, really.

"He'll be walking along the waterfront," Margaret repeated herself. "He always walks to his office. It's about two miles, just on the other side of the old Westside Pier. Hedgeley and Kirkham. They have their own little building there on Front Street. Seventeen seventy Front Street."

"Thanks," Sapphire said, rising to leave.

"He doesn't want to see you," Margaret said.

"I know that," Sapphire said. "He's made it perfectly plain already. Trouble is, I'm not going to give him a choice."

"The thing keeps coming around," Margaret said. "Ever since Dan Fulsom tried to kill Argus."

"Tried to kill him?" Sapphire interrupted. "I thought Fulsom killed himself?"

"He did, the same day, the day he was caught. Poisoned himself in his cell. He'd gone crazy, you know, kept rambling about how there were dragons living under the city, dragons that had to be fed. He'd been going around having homeless people murdered as part of his scheme. Then he laid some sort of a trap for Argus and tried to shoot him, but Argus' friends saved the day. That was luck."

"I had no idea," Sapphire shook her head. "I wonder why I never heard about that."

"They hushed it all up," Margaret said. "Fulsom had friends in high places, and since he went and offed himself, there was really no need to let everyone know what was what. Rumor had it there were officials who were looking the other way when he was only going after those street people. I don't really mean 'only'. It was awful, but you know what I mean."

"Fulsom was always lucky too, if by lucky you mean he paid everyone off. It was how he got his way every time. It was how he got Snapdragon Alley in the first place."

"Argus told me about that too, in his way. I don't think he’s ever told me everything, though. That's one reason I wanted to talk to you," Margaret said. "You were there. I have my own theories, but I've always wanted to know what you thought."

Sapphire wondered what Margaret meant by 'theories'. Was she some sort of amateur sleuth? Maybe a mystic or religious believer? Maybe she had too much time on her hands. The conversation could begin to get weird, Sapphire thought. After all, she had no theories herself.

"I don't want to keep you from whatever it is that you do," Sapphire said, thinking that maybe she could get out of it now.

"Oh, I have no classes today," Margaret said.

"You're in school?" Sapphire asked. "What are you studying?"

"Not quite," Margaret laughed. "I'm a professor. I teach nuclear physics at New Harbinger College."

"Oh," Sapphire said, startled. "Wow."

"Yeah, wow," Margaret chuckled. "But what do you think? What did you think at the time?"

"Well, the way I remember it," Sapphire said, "is like this. We first found out about Snapdragon Alley when Argus noticed it on a bus transit map. It was only there for one year. Alex had all of the maps. He was funny that way. The following year it was gone. We thought that was kind of weird, but actually it wasn't. It was Fulsom. He already had plans to build his shopping mall and football stadium there so the fix was in with the city, it was all a done deal. That’s why it was put on the map. Only it turned out there was an old man who still lived there and he wouldn't sell, so the deal didn’t go through. At the same time, Fulsom got busted for some other bit of corruption so the plan went on hold. When he got out of prison, though, he went right back to work, to get the old man out of the way. The old man, Mason, was still holding out. You see, his wife disappeared, and he said she went into what was some kind of portal, or wormhole or something, right there in what they called Snapdragon Alley. Alex and Argus' Uncle Charlie said he did too, only it was different with him. With Henrietta, the thing showed itself like a nice little neighborhood. With Charlie it came in the shape of a bus, because he was a bus driver see? And she liked gardening or something like that. Anyway, it was all probably nothing. Charlie was being really weird this one day and he ran out into the street, and Argus followed after him. I don't know why, but I got suddenly scared and ran after Argus. I caught up to him and grabbed him, he was kicking and fussing, and when he got all calmed down we noticed Charlie was gone. Now, Charlie, he had vanished before, and he could have gone anywhere. I wasn't paying attention. Alex tells me he never came back, though, not after that."

Sapphire paused to catch her breath. It was all coming back to her, as vivid as the day it occurred, and she was totally convinced now, as she was then, that there was nothing unusual about it. The boy could have been hit by a car. That had to be all she was thinking. The other stuff was just completely insane.

"That's pretty close to how Argus tells it," Margaret said thoughtfully, "only he saw the bus too, and he saw Charlie get in it."

"What bus?" Sapphire said. "There couldn't have been a bus. It wasn't even a street, and the bus didn't run there."

"He saw it," Margaret explained. "It didn't 'run there', you're right, it came out of nowhere, according to Argus. It simply appeared and then it was gone."

"I don't believe it," said Sapphire. "And I never did. Charlie was saying it was like another dimension, where there isn't any time, or something like that. There couldn't be any such place."

"Maybe not," Margaret said, "but maybe it's more like a thing than a place, a creature, perhaps, like Dan Fulsom's dragon."

"What are you talking about?" Sapphire asked. She was beginning to think her fears were about to come true, more wild-eyed, superstitious nonsense, just like all the crap on TV.

"Well," Margaret said slowly, "it's only a theory, but here's what I think. It's a creature, and somehow it's stuck. It doesn't belong in this world, or maybe it does, I don't know, but it's stuck, and maybe it's hurt. I think Fulsom was wrong about the thing being hungry, but he was right about it being a thing. I think it's alone and it's lonely. I think, and I know this is all based on practically nothing, but I think that it senses whatever's around it, it can pick up some signals, maybe brain waves or thoughts, and it sends out these snares, like the bus, like the girl. You think I'm crazy now, don't you?"

Sapphire didn't answer right away. She didn't want to offend this nice person, especially since it was Argus' wife and she was going to need her, sooner or later. On the other hand, she did think the woman was probably nuts. But she couldn't be sure. Nuclear physics? Obviously the woman was smart, and she didn't sound crazy. She talked like she'd thought the thing through, but did it make any sense? Sapphire drank some more coffee to give herself time to keep thinking.

"Why Argus?" she finally asked.

"He was there," Margaret quickly replied. "He was there when it went after Charlie with the bus, and it sensed him, so it knew something about him."

"They put a stadium there," Sapphire countered. "It must have sensed millions of people if that's how it works."

"Maybe it goes dormant," Margaret replied. She had obviously considered this angle.

"It goes dormant," she continued. "Look at the pattern. It was seventeen years after Charlie when Fulsom went after Argus, and now? It's been seventeen years again now."

Sapphire wished she'd thought of recording this conversation, but at the time it didn't seem like that was going to be needed. Now she had to wonder. Maybe there was something to this theory. At the very least it was an angle to the story. She reached into her pocket to pull out her device. She was going to ask Margaret to repeat her ideas when her phone rang instead. It was Sneed.

"We've got trouble," Sneed shouted. "The girl, or whatever it is, she’s gone."

Robbed of his sense of sight, Casey struggled to find the exit. He had wandered around the room aimlessly until he finally reached an exit tunnel. That, however, was only the beginning. He also had to navigate a maze of tunnels until he finally reached a set of stairs.

He reached the top of them without having a clue where he was. He continued on his way until he finally reached the open air. He turned around and gasped. He stood in front of another Maya temple! It was distinctly different from the one where camp was. The Maya must’ve had a huge underground network connecting all of their establishments. No wonder they used to be able to get around so fast.

As he gazed off into the distance, he thought he recognized the glow of camp. He headed off in that direction, forgetting everything that Roberto had said about going through the jungle at night. In the next few hours, he would regret his decision.

He was slowly walking through the jungle when the chirping started. It was a shrill sound that stabbed his heart with fear. He moved faster until he stumbled over a rock and fell, grazing his hands and knees. When he got up, something was eerily different. Then he realized what it was. There wasn’t any more chirping. Somehow, that was more frightening than the chirping itself.

With no warning the leaves next to him parted, and thousands upon thousands of crickets poured out. Casey stumbled back, and then sprinted as fast as he could. When he couldn’t hear the menacing crickets anymore, he stopped and sat down on a rock. He sat there for a good, long while, waiting for his heart rate to return to normal.

If it hadn’t have been for the crickets, he would have died. While sitting on the rock, he heard the muffled sound of crickets. He quickly climbed on top of the rock, only to be confused when nothing jumped at him. Then, as if appearing out of nowhere, a huge anaconda lunged at him. He just managed to avoid it, and once again started sprinting. It must have gorged itself on the crickets and then come after him.

He had never been so terrified and was about to curl into a little ball and cry when he suddenly burst through the trees into camp. He nearly cried as he rushed into his father’s waiting arms.

"It's a living," Alex shrugged. He was seated with his back to the door, across the table from Sapphire in the only diner in Two Forks, Arizona. He wasn't terribly surprised how quickly she'd tracked him down. He'd always known Sapphire to get what she wanted, whenever she wanted. She told him it had only taken one phone call to find him there in what anyone would say was the middle of nowhere. Two Forks was not even a bend in the road, but a ditch on the side of an empty straight line that went on for miles. Alex and Carmela, the waitress, were the only two people in the town that afternoon when Sapphire arrived by rental car. She didn't know why she hadn't gone straight to the scene of the story but had detoured at least a hundred miles to see her old friend. Maybe she thought he could fill her in on some angle that would be more interesting than the one being plastered all over the TV and news outlets by the other seven thousand reporters who'd gathered around the damn sinkhole. At this point, she hadn't even admitted to him why she was there.

She'd come into the diner, spotted a balding, slightly chubby middle-aged man examining a sandwich and figured it had to be Alex, so she walked over and planted herself in a chair and took a closer look. Same pale eyes but that was about all she could recognize. Alex, however, knew her in an instant.

"Well, well, Sapphire Karadjian, right here in Two Forks. Who'd a thunk it?" he smiled, and held out her hand. They shook briefly and she smiled back.

"So you’re a railroad safety inspector," she said.

"It's a living." he shrugged, "and anyway, it suits me. I get to travel around," he added with a wave of his hand, indicating the desert around them, "and I get to meet people," he continued, nodding in the direction of Carmela, who was busily washing a spoon. She waved back but didn't speak.

"Carmela's good people," Alex mentioned confidingly.

"But what do you do?" Sapphire persisted.

"Always the ace reporter," Alex winked. "Curious about everything, always. Same as it ever was. Same as it ever was."

"I'm supposing you inspect trains," she went on undeterred.

"Crossings, mostly," he said, "making sure that they work. You wouldn't want cars getting themselves launched by a freight because the arm didn't go down or the bells didn't sound. You want to make sure things are shipshape forever."

"And you cover a region, I suppose?"

"The whole state," Alex said. "Know it backwards and forwards by now."

"Knowing you, you've probably marked it all off on a map," Sapphire laughed.

"Oh, I have," he replied, "only now I've been everywhere so many times it's hardly worth bothering about. Funny thing, though. I've hardly been out of the state. Been to Mexico a few times but that's about it. Texas, once. California."

"What about family?" Sapphire wanted to know.

"Well, I know all there is about you," Alex said. "See you on TV now and then. Guess it's only fair you wouldn't know a thing about me."

"It goes on," Sapphire shrugged.

"That's for sure," he replied. "Say, would you like a cup of coffee? Carmela? Cup of coffee, por favor?"

"Dos," he continued as Sapphire nodded and Carmela came over swiftly with their order.

"I have seen you on the TV too," she told Sapphire. "You're even more beautiful in person."

"I am?" Sapphire blinked a couple of times. "Nobody ever says that!"

"I do," said Carmela as she walked slowly back to the counter. Sapphire shook her head a couple of times, wondering if she'd really just heard it.

"Gets pretty lonely out here," Alex quietly said, and then louder, after taking a sip, he went on.

"Myself, I'm divorced. Father of two, though, father of two. Teenagers, both of them, Charlie and Connie. Good kids, more or less."

"A boy and a girl, eh? Every parents dream."

"No, they're both girls," Alex said. "Charlie is short for Charlotte. Wanted a boy, you know. Wanted to name him after my uncle, but a girl's what we got, so we made it as close as we could. She always liked being called Charlie, you know. Connie, on the other hand, wants to be called Cookie these days. Says she's going to run off and join the navy just as soon as she can."

"How old is she now?"

"Fourteen," Alex said, "and Charlie's seventeen. Both of them got minds of their own, tell you that. Got it from their mother, Gretchen. She's a piece of work, I'll tell you."

"Would I know her?" Sapphire asked. It was possible, after all. She might have gone to school with the girl.

"Doubt it," said Alex. "I met her at college, in Tucson. She'd come there from Boulder, which is where she is now, with my girls. Don't hardly ever see 'em these days, but I'm well aware of them each and every payday, when more than half of what I get I don't get."

"Been divorced long?" Sapphire knew she was prying.

"Oh yeah," Alex said, "been a very long time."

"And you never re-married?"

"Not hardly gonna do that again!" Alex laughed. "I can hardly afford the first one, so what would I do with another?"

"You're looking good, though," Sapphire said, feeling she had to say something more friendly.

"I look in the mirror every morning," Alex chided her. "But you didn't come here for this. Come to think of it, I can hardly imagine what you did come here for? I thought you were out there in the Republic of Guano or whatever it is."

"Guyana," Sapphire said. "I wish I was there."

"No offense," she added quickly, sensing her faux pas. "It's great to see you. Really, it is."

"You didn't come here for me," Alex repeated.

"Not only," Sapphire put her hand to her forehead. It was certainly sticky and hot in that place.

"It's the sinkhole," she muttered.

"The sinkhole?" Alex seemed to be surprised. "They assigned YOU to a SINKHOLE? Who's going to do the real news if not you?"

"Thanks," Sapphire managed a smile. "I appreciate the sentiment."

"But I mean it," Alex added. "I was thinking there must be some global conspiracy happening right around here, since you showed up, but the sinkhole? Hell, it's a hole in the ground. So it's volcanic, I get it. The thing is unusual, but they've got the place covered with cameras. It's a tabloid affair. Not for you. Not for Sapphire Karadjian!"

"Just following orders," she murmured sheepishly, but inwardly she felt gratified that someone at least recognized her true value.

"It's probably because of the girl," Alex said.

"The girl?"

"Yep, the girl," Alex sat back in his chair. He had information, and knew it, information that someone like Sapphire would pay for. He sat there wondering how much he should charge. After all, she WAS an old friend. There might be a discount in that.

"Not many people actually know about her," he continued. "It's sort of hush-hush. Those who do know have been told to clam up. I've been told to clam up. Not supposed to be mentioning it, especially not to someone like you," he said, and then he clammed up. Sapphire was a veteran at this. It was as if she was reading his thoughts.

"There'll be something in it for you," she promised. "Guaranteed. The bosses pay my expenses. So tell me, what about this girl?"

Alex considered for a few moments, looking away from Sapphire. He turned to his left, and then shifted his chair to the right. He caught sight of Carmela and grinned. She grinned back, and then he looked back at Sapphire and said,

"Let's go for a walk."

They got up. Alex left a twenty-dollar bill on the table - far more than a sandwich and coffees would cost - and with a slight bow to the waitress, walked out of the diner, followed by his childhood companion.

"I might take another look at that crossing," he said, pointing down the road to where some old freight tracks came over the highway. Sapphire got the picture. Alex wanted no witnesses. Maybe there was something to this story after all.

As the center piece to the calendar fell into place, there was a sound like thunder, and then it began to glow around the edges. James stepped closer to get a better look. The calendar depicted a scene of what appeared to be spaceships coming to Earth. James stood up from his crouched position and moved back from the calendar. “Roberto, call whoever is in command of the army, and tell them that aliens are coming to Earth.”

“Sir?” said Roberto.

“Do as I say!” shouted James. Just then, Casey ran in.

“Dad! I had a horrible dream, and I just know that something bad is going to hap..” He cut off mid-sentence when he noticed the glowing calendar. “Is that..?”

“Yes, son, that is the Maya calendar. The complete one, I should say. It shows spaceships coming down to Earth. But don’t worry, we’ve already warned the army.”

“You’re basing all this on a stupid Calendar?” exclaimed Casey. “What if it isn’t right? What if they’re not coming to attack us?”

“Casey, calm down. I know what I’m talking about. You just need rest. Go lay down.” Furiously, Casey stormed out. Later that day, the army rolled into camp.

By now Casey was used to waking up in strange places, so when he woke up and took in a deep breath of jungle air, he wasn’t surprised. He got out of his hammock, stretched, and went to find his father. He found him sleeping in his tent and looked at his clock. It was five o’clock in the morning, and the jungle birds had begun to chirp. Then, unable to restrain himself any longer, he wrapped his arms around his dad. His dad started awake, turned over, and saw Casey.

“Casey! It’s only five o’clock! What’s wrong?” his dad exclaimed.

“Dad! I’ve missed you!” Casey sobbed back.

“What do you mean? You saw me just before we went to sleep!”

“It’s a really long story,” Casey exhaled. “You need to wake everyone up right now and tell them that the Maya are coming! Don’t let the army attack them, though, or else they will destroy Earth! Please just trust me this once.”

“Casey, how could you possibly know that?”

“Dad, please.” Casey knew that his dad would never believe him, but he tried none the less. “You saw the calendar, and you know what was on it. But the Maya aren’t coming to start a war. Please just give me a chance to talk to them.”

“All right Casey, now just go back to bed.” From his tone Casey could tell that he didn’t believe him and was just agreeing to get him to leave. Knowing that he could never convince his dad, he played along with it and left the tent. The chilled morning air bit through the light hoodie he was wearing, but soon the first morning light peeked through the trees and slowly began to warm him to the bone.

Casey made his way over to a rock that baked in the morning sun and sat down to contemplate what would happen that afternoon. He knew that somehow he had to stop the attack. The only problem was that Casey didn’t know what they wanted. He sat there on that rock for a good well over two hours before the answer hit him so hard it knocked the wind out of him, literally.

It happened so swiftly that Casey could barely comprehend it. The little orb flew out of his pocket and hit him in his chest, knocking him off of the rock. It sat there on his chest, perched like a little bird, ready to take flight at any moment.

Slowly, Casey reached up and grasped the little silver ball with both of his hands so that it wouldn’t attack him again. As the warmth of the orb flowed through his body, understanding dawned on him. That was it. That was why the Maya had come to Earth in the first place. They wanted the orb. And that meant that this whole conundrum was his fault.

When Casey woke up, he knew something was different. He couldn’t remember what had happened to him at first, but then it all started coming back: The giant warship, getting knocked unconscious by the Maya... Then it dawned on him. They could have easily killed him then and there, yet here he stood perfectly unharmed apart from a small headache. He didn’t have time to ponder it though because a different thought struck him.

He had no idea where he currently was. He noticed a tinted window and looked out of the small room he was in. Outside was an empty void, twinkling with little points of light. Casey gave a start when he realized that he was in space. He ran to the window and looked out. Planets and constellations he had never seen before dotted the dark canvas.

An icy feeling began to crawl across Casey’s skin as he realized that the Maya had jumped back through the wormhole. He panicked and ran to what he assumed was a door and pounded on it with his fists. Finally, exhausted and breathing heavily from so much banging, he slumped down next to the door, defeated.

*Boop... Boop... Boop.* Casey looked up. The little window had become darkened, and was now displaying an image. It must have been some sort of screen. Upon further examination, he realized what the picture was. It displayed a lot of symbols that were unfamiliar to him, but in the center was a shape that was unmistakable—the orb that he was carrying in his pocket at that very moment. He reached into his pocket and took it out. Remembering what the automaton had said, he knew it must be important. As a matter of fact, as he examined it up close he could see different glowing, multicolored lines.

With a slithering sound like a snake, the door slid up into the ceiling. Casey jumped back in fear as a group of Maya entered the room. They had firearms in their hands, and Casey knew that this was the end. They had come to kill him. Remembering the orb, he brought it out in front of him as if threatening the Maya. Fear flashed in their eyes as they backed away in awe.

Casey knew that he had nothing left to lose. Having no idea what it would do, Casey twisted the orb on a random set of lines. All the air got sucked out of his lungs as a swirling portal materialized out of thin air. Knowing there was no better alternative, Casey jumped through the portal. The last sentient thought that he had was wishing he was home. He felt all the blood drain from his head and he lost consciousness.

Casey loved the smell of bacon. He wanted to stay in bed, but the smell began to overpower his taste buds and make him crave the salty meat. As if struck by lightning, he jumped out of bed and ran downstairs to the kitchen. He found his dad frying bacon and ran over to give him a hug.

“I’ve missed you Dad,” he said.

“I’ve missed you, too, Casey. So, tell me exactly what happened yesterday.”

Had it really only been yesterday? To Casey it seemed like an eternity ago. He noticed his dad was waiting for him to sit down to the scrumptious breakfast he had made him. After breakfast, Casey explained the whole story of what had happened to him. He talked about how the Maya had captured him, how he had gone back in time, and finally how he had saved the world. His dad explained how Casey had collapsed into unconsciousness and how he had brought him home. The medics had suggested they bring him to the hospital, but James knew that Casey wouldn’t like that. They had agreed to let him stay at home as long as he told them everything when he was well enough.

Casey, on the other hand, was feeling perfectly fine. He knew that he would eventually have to tell the government everything, but for now he just sat and talked with his dad. It was late in the afternoon when Casey said that he was feeling tired and decided to retire to bed. He had just flopped onto his bed when he realized he was wearing the same clothes from yesterday. At the same moment he felt a strange lump in his pocket.

He slowly reached into his pocket and brought out a small square box that fit in the palm of his hand. It had markings on the sides that looked remarkably like the ones on the orb. Realizing that it must be the object the Mayan had tossed at him, he vaguely remembered slipping it into his pocket. Upon closer inspection, he saw that it had a small red button attached to the top. With growing excitement he noticed tiny little letters written in a flowing golden script. The inscription read: *In case you change your mind.*

Casey was in the middle of telling James all about his adventures, when another excavation crew member entered. “Sir, we found the other part of the calendar,” then, seeing Casey, he said a little awkwardly, “Oh, I didn’t mean to intrude or anything, sir. Welcome back kid.” With that, he turned on his heel and was gone.

“I’ll talk to the excavation crew about uncovering this Maya Underground, but right now, I need to go see this calendar.” He turned away to leave, but then turned back, looked Casey in the eyes, and said, “I’m so glad you’re back, Kiddo.” Then he was gone.

Casey went over to his bed and curled up in the blanket. It felt coarse against his grazed knees. Slowly, he fell into an unsure sleep.

Fire. It was all around him, pouring down on all sides. He had no sense of direction, only that he must go forward. He ran, and dodged the burning trees that fell in his path. He needed to escape. He had to escape. Then, he saw his father standing over a large disc. “Dad!” he shouted. James didn’t turn, but instead a huge block of burning stone fell in between him and his dad.

Then he felt a strange warmth in his pocket. He put his hand inside, and brought out the silver orb. Glowing lines covered its surface. He threw it into the fire, and the world exploded into shards of light.

Casey woke up in a cold sweat. *How am I alive?* he thought. Then he realized that he had been dreaming. He felt something warm in his pocket and took out the little silver orb. It was glowing. Suddenly, he jumped up and ran to go find his dad.
